Consultant Neurologist,  

Daniel Harris, DOB: 14-03-1986, Hospital No: K917204 NHS No. 7489203156  
Flat 12, Mariners Court, 8 Dockside Way, London, SE16 3AB

Thank you for asking me to review this gentleman. We conducted a planned telephone consultation while he was onshore between offshore rotations. He reports a longstanding history of generalised epilepsy. He may go four to five days without seizures, but when they happen he often has them in batches, with two - three occurring within 24 hours. He and his partner describe typical events as abrupt loss of awareness with generalised stiffening and rhythmic jerking lasting around 60–90 seconds, followed by post-ictal confusion for up to 30 minutes. He occasionally bites his tongue and has had one shoulder strain in the past but no recent injuries. There is no consistent focal onset aura reported.

He works offshore on a two-weeks-on, two-weeks-off rotation. Seizures tend to cluster either at the end of a run of night shifts or within the first 48 hours after returning onshore, which he attributes to sleep disruption and variable meal times. He denies alcohol excess and states he avoids caffeine late in the day. He uses a medication alarm and a written seizure log while offshore. Occupational Health have placed him on restricted duties when offshore; he confirms he does not undertake safety-critical tasks on days following a seizure.

He is currently taking valproate 1,000 mg twice daily and levetiracetam 1,500 mg twice daily with good adherence. No clear adverse effects are reported beyond mild irritability during periods of poor sleep. He has rescue buccal midazolam available but has not needed to use it in the last three months. He has not driven and understands DVLA regulations. He last had a generalised tonic–clonic seizure 10 days ago, with two events occurring the same day, and none since. 

Past EEGs (most recently last year) showed generalised spike-and-wave discharges consistent with a generalised epilepsy syndrome; prior MRI brain was normal. There is no family history of epilepsy known. He has had no recent infections, head injuries, or changes in prescribed medication.

Impression: Generalised epilepsy with clustering related to sleep disruption and rota transitions. Current regimen is broadly effective with intermittent breakthrough clusters as described above. We discussed optimising sleep hygiene during shift transitions and maintaining strict regularity of doses while offshore. He prefers to continue the present regimen for now. We agreed to continue telephone reviews when he is onshore, with the option of bringing him for a routine EEG update in the next 6–9 months if breakthrough clusters increase. He will contact the clinic sooner if he experiences prolonged seizures, increased frequency, or any injuries.

Plan:
- Continue valproate 1,000 mg twice daily and levetiracetam 1,500 mg twice daily.
- Maintain rescue midazolam for prolonged seizures (>5 minutes) and cluster management per prior plan.
- Reinforce sleep and shift-transition strategies; continue seizure diary.
- Occupational Health restrictions to remain unchanged offshore.
- Telephone review during his next onshore period in approximately 8–10 weeks, or earlier if seizures escalate.

Yours sincerely

KINGS NEUROSCIENCES CENTRE


Clinic Date: 02 October 2025

Dr A. Rahman
The Lime Tree Health Centre

14 Willow Street

Kent BR1 2AB
Dear Dr A. Rahman
Thomas Green, DOB: 09-02-1991, Hospital No: H927461 NHS No. 7452019863
Flat 3, 12 Millbank Court, Bromley, BR1 4JP 

Diagnoses/summary: Combined generalised and focal epilepsy (patient describes both generalised tonic–clonic seizures and focal impaired-awareness events), seizure pattern exacerbated by circadian disruption from rotating night shifts

MRI brain 2018 reported structurally normal brain; routine EEG 2018 showed intermittent generalised spike–wave with occasional left temporal sharp transients; sleep-deprived EEG 2021 with generalised polyspike–wave and rare left temporal spikes, consistent with combined generalised and focal epileptiform activity

Previous medication: Valproate (effective for generalised seizures but stopped due to weight gain and tremor), Carbamazepine (worsened generalised discharges), Levetiracetam (behavioural irritability), Lamotrigine (partial benefit), Clobazam PRN (helpful for clusters but sedation), Topiramate (word-finding difficulty), Zonisamide (insomnia), Lacosamide (limited benefit), Perampanel (mood effects)

Not taken: Brivaracetam, Cenobamate, Rufinamide, Ethosuximide, Pregabalin, Tiagabine

Other background: Shift-based employment including nights; longstanding irregular sleep; no history of significant head injury; no family history of epilepsy; does not drive

I reviewed Thomas Green in clinic today. He attended alone and provided a detailed diary covering the past three months. He reports that sleep disruption from rotating shifts is a major trigger. He may go four days without seizures, but when they happen he often has them in batches, with three occurring within 24 hours. Within these clusters he typically experiences brief focal impaired-awareness episodes (staring, automatisms, loss of awareness for 1–2 minutes) sometimes preceded by an epigastric rising sensation, and on some occasions these are followed later the same day by a generalised tonic–clonic seizure. He also describes occasional early-morning generalised seizures after consecutive night shifts. Post-ictally he is fatigued with myalgia and mild confusion for several hours.

Current medication:
- Lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily
- Levetiracetam 1 g twice daily
- Clobazam 10 mg at night PRN for clusters (used approximately twice monthly)

Adverse effects: reports irritability on levetiracetam mitigated somewhat with dose timing and exercise; otherwise tolerating regimen. No recent injuries. He remains abstinent from alcohol on working weeks and drinks minimal caffeine.

Examination today: Neurological examination normal. Weight stable, BMI 24. No focal deficits. Blood pressure 122/76.

Investigations: U&Es, LFTs, FBC from August 2025 normal; Vitamin D borderline low (51 nmol/L). No evidence of hyponatraemia. ECG last year normal sinus rhythm.

Discussion/Plan:
- We discussed that his pattern and investigations support a diagnosis of combined generalised and focal epilepsy. We reviewed the role of sleep and circadian stability; he is a rotating shift worker including nights and feels the night-to-day swing is the principal precipitant of clusters.
- Medication: continue Lamotrigine 150 mg BD. Reduce Levetiracetam to 750 mg BD trial if mood symptoms persist after we implement sleep measures; if seizures worsen, revert to 1 g BD. Consider Brivaracetam as a future alternative if irritability remains problematic. Continue Clobazam 10 mg nocte PRN at onset of cluster for up to 3 nights; he understands the sedation risk.
- Rescue/cluster plan: maintain diary; if three or more focal events occur in 24 hours, he will take Clobazam that night and prioritise sleep recovery. He has agreed to call the epilepsy nurse line if clusters persist beyond 48 hours or any injury occurs.
- Occupational guidance: provided a written note supporting trial of forward-rotating shifts and at least two consecutive recovery sleep periods after nights; he will discuss with his employer’s occupational health team. We covered safety at work and at home (showers rather than baths, avoid heights/ladders alone, caution with machinery when sleep-deprived).
- Driving: not driving currently; we reiterated DVLA regulations and the need to inform DVLA if applicable.
- Lifestyle: advised consistent sleep window on off-duty days, morning light exposure after night shifts, and limiting caffeine after midday. Vitamin D supplementation 1000 IU daily suggested given borderline level (over the counter acceptable).
- Further investigations: none urgently required. If control remains suboptimal after schedule adjustments, we will discuss ambulatory EEG to better characterise sleep-related triggers and consider Brivaracetam or Cenobamate depending on response and tolerability.

Follow-up: Epilepsy nurse telephone follow-up in 6 weeks to review shift adjustments, mood, and cluster frequency; clinic review in 4 months or earlier if clusters increase in frequency or if he has any generalised seizures despite improved sleep strategy.

Please do not hesitate to contact me if further information is required. Thank you for your ongoing care.

Yours sincerely

Department of Neurology (Adult Services)

Clinic Date: 02 October 2025

Dr Patel
St Mary's Hospital
Department of Neurology, St Mary's Hospital, London W2 1NY

Dear Dr Patel,

Re: Emily Carter, DOB: 17-08-1989, Hospital No: C672154, NHS No: 4728395612
78 Willow Lane, London, W9 3HT

Thank you for referring Emily Carter, who has recently transitioned from paediatric to adult neurology services. On this occasion she attended with her mother, who contributed collateral history. She has a known diagnosis of focal epilepsy, with semiology consistent with focal impaired-awareness seizures arising from the temporal region by history.

Current medication:
- Lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily
- Levetiracetam 1,000 mg twice daily

Previous treatments (patient-reported):
- Carbamazepine (discontinued due to dizziness and diplopia)
- Topiramate (discontinued for cognitive side effects)

History since transition and interval events:
Following the recent medication adjustment, focal impaired-awareness seizures have been occurring more often, 3 times per week, whereas previously they only happened once or twice a month. The patient and her mother describe typical events beginning with a rising epigastric sensation and déjà vu, followed by impaired awareness with unresponsiveness and automatisms lasting 1–2 minutes, and fatigue thereafter for up to an hour. There have been no generalised tonic–clonic seizures reported. No injuries or rescue medication use. Triggers noted by the patient include poor sleep and high academic stress since starting college.

Adherence and tolerability:
She reports full adherence. No rash, mood change beyond mild irritability possibly related to levetiracetam, and no cognitive complaints on the current lamotrigine dose. Sleep pattern is irregular during examination periods.

Examination:
General and neurological examinations today are unremarkable. Vitals stable.

Investigations to date (summary from paediatric records and transfer documents):
- MRI brain (age 15): structurally normal study.
- EEGs (most recent age 17): left temporal interictal epileptiform discharges.

Assessment:
Focal epilepsy with worsening focal impaired-awareness seizure frequency temporally associated with the recent medication adjustment during transition to adult services. Collateral history is consistent and there is no suggestion of new precipitants other than sleep disruption and stress.

Plan:
- We discussed optimising lifestyle factors (sleep regularity, stress management) and maintaining a seizure diary with clear documentation of time, context, and recovery features. The patient will also document any menstrual association, although she does not currently report a cyclical pattern.
- We will obtain updated bloods including FBC, U&Es, LFTs, vitamin D, and lamotrigine level for context only.
- We reviewed SUDEP risk and standard safety advice (bathing supervision where appropriate, cooking precautions, and driving restrictions as per DVLA guidance). She is not currently driving.
- No immediate change to prescription today while we complete levels and review diary data; we will bring her to the next available epilepsy MDT to consider dose optimisation or rationalisation of therapy.
- Follow-up in 8 weeks, sooner if events escalate or if she experiences any generalised convulsive seizures.

Thank you for your ongoing support with transition care. Please let us know if there are concerns from your side. We will copy this letter to the patient and her mother with consent.

Yours sincerely,

Department of Neurology 

Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 

Dr Amelia Clarke  
St Bartholomew’s Hospital  
Department of Neurology, West Smithfield, London EC1A 7BE  

Dear Dr Amelia Clarke,  

Michael Turner, DOB: 22-03-1990, Hospital No: H492817 NHS No. 9438257612  
Flat 3, 12 Arundel Court, Shoreditch, London E2 7PA 

Diagnoses: 

Focal epilepsy with focal impaired-awareness seizures, onset 2017. MRI brain (2018) normal. Interictal EEG (2019) left temporal sharp waves. 

Current Medication: 

Levetiracetam 1,000 mg twice daily  
Lacosamide 100 mg twice daily 

Plan: 

- Optimise antiseizure therapy: increase Lacosamide to 150 mg twice daily, continue Levetiracetam 1,000 mg twice daily  
- Seizure diary and trigger management; occupational risk mitigation advice provided  
- DVLA guidance discussed and workplace safety measures advised given strobe/bright light exposure  
- Occupational Health referral and employer liaison letter offered (with patient consent)  
- Follow-up in 8–10 weeks, sooner if events worsen 

I reviewed Michael Turner, a stage lighting technician with frequent exposure to strobe and bright lighting, in my clinic today. He reports a longstanding history of focal epilepsy, supported by prior EEG evidence of left temporal sharp waves and a structurally normal MRI. Following the recent medication adjustment, focal impaired-awareness seizures have been occurring more often, several times per week, whereas previously they only happened once or twice a month. He describes a typical warning of a rising epigastric sensation and déjà vu, followed by impaired awareness and automatisms lasting approximately 1–2 minutes, with post-event fatigue. Colleagues have occasionally witnessed episodes during rigging and rehearsal, prompting safety concerns in the work environment. There have been no generalised tonic-clonic seizures. 

He denies medication non-adherence, sleep deprivation is intermittent during show runs, and he has noted that high-frequency strobe sequences and prolonged bright light exposure can precede events. There is no new head injury, intercurrent illness, or alcohol excess. Neurological examination today was normal. 

We discussed optimising therapy given the clear increase in event frequency temporally associated with the recent regimen change. I have advised increasing Lacosamide to 150 mg twice daily while continuing Levetiracetam 1,000 mg twice daily, with monitoring for dizziness, diplopia, mood change, or rash. He will maintain a detailed seizure diary noting timing, potential light exposure patterns, sleep, hydration, and missed meals. 

Given his role and potential exposure to strobe effects, I provided tailored workplace advice: avoid working at height, hot truss, and live power tasks without direct supervision; avoid solo work during programming; and request colleagues to use a calm verbal cue, protect him from falls, and time events if witnessed. We discussed DVLA guidance owing to focal impaired-awareness seizures, and I encouraged him to review the current regulations and contact the DVLA as applicable. With consent, I have offered to write to Occupational Health and his employer to support reasonable adjustments and risk mitigation. 

I will review him in 8–10 weeks to assess response to the dose adjustment. He will contact the clinic sooner if seizures escalate, become prolonged, or if any new red flag features occur. 

With best wishes,

KINGS NEUROSCIENCES CENTRE

Clinic Date: 02 October 2025

Dr A. Rahman
Elmfield Health Centre

12 Elmfield Road, Bromley, Kent BR1 1LR

Dear Dr A. Rahman

Jordan Ellis, DOB: 14-03-1990, Hospital No: H729384 NHS No. 8429165032
Flat 3, Oakview Supported Living, 22 Meadow Lane, Bromley BR2 8AX

Diagnoses/summary: Combined generalised and focal epilepsy – the patient has both generalised and focal epilepsy. Prior video-EEG has captured focal onset events with impaired awareness and separate generalised tonic-clonic seizures without clear focal onset. Lives in supported accommodation where rotating staff maintain seizure charts, which were reviewed today and used as the primary source of frequency data.

Current issues: Following the recent medication adjustment, focal impaired-awareness seizures have been occurring more often, 2 times per week, whereas previously they only happened once or twice a month. Staff notes also document two generalised tonic-clonic seizures over the past eight weeks, both occurring from sleep, with tongue bite and postictal confusion lasting approximately 30–40 minutes. No reported injuries. Mood is stable by patient report; no new visual symptoms or cognitive decline noted by staff. Appetite and weight stable.

Investigations: Prior MRI (2019) non-lesional. Routine EEG (2023) showed intermittent left temporal sharp waves and separate generalised spike–wave discharges during hyperventilation, consistent with combined generalised and focal epilepsy.

Current medication: Lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily; Levetiracetam 1,000 mg twice daily; Folic acid 5 mg once daily. No known drug allergies. Adherence supported by blister packs administered by accommodation staff; no missed doses recorded on charts in the last month.

Background/social: Supported accommodation with rotating staff. Staff maintain daily seizure charts, which reliably capture witnessed events; they also log potential triggers (sleep disruption, intercurrent illness). Patient attends a community day programme three times weekly and walks daily with support worker. No alcohol or recreational drugs reported.

Examination today: Alert and cooperative. Neurological examination non-focal. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations unremarkable. BMI within healthy range. No injuries noted.

Impression: Combined generalised and focal epilepsy with recent increase in focal impaired-awareness seizure frequency following a medication adjustment, while generalised tonic-clonic events remain infrequent. Charts suggest good adherence and adequate sleep; no clear precipitant identified.

Plan:
- Continue current antiepileptic regimen pending review of the precise timing and nature of the recent adjustment (staff to provide copy of MAR sheet and date of dose change).
- Request seizure chart copies for the last 12 weeks to correlate events with the adjustment timeline and potential triggers.
- Bloods: U&Es, LFTs, FBC, bone profile, lamotrigine level, and levetiracetam level to check for subtherapeutic or fluctuating concentrations.
- Safety: Reinforced seizure first aid with staff; nocturnal supervision to continue; advised use of protective measures in bathroom and kitchen per current care plan.
- Follow-up: Nurse specialist telephone review in 4–6 weeks to reassess frequency from charts and patient report; clinic review in 3 months, sooner if generalised seizures increase or injuries occur.

Thank you for your ongoing support and for facilitating sharing of the MAR sheets and seizure charts from the supported accommodation team.

Yours sincerely

Epilepsy Centre 

Neurosciences Division 

Clinic Date: 21 September 2025 

Dr Patel  
St. Cuthbert Community Health Centre  
42 Mill Lane, Newcastle upon Tyne, NE3 4HT  

Dear Dr Patel,  

Laura Bennett, DOB: 14-02-1991, Hospital No: NHS5482031 NHS No. 8374629501  
Flat 3, 19 Orchard Close, Newcastle upon Tyne, NE2 5LP  

Diagnoses: 

Symptomatic generalised epilepsy.

I reviewed Laura Bennett in clinic today with her partner present. She has a confirmed history of generalised epilepsy and remains under our service for ongoing management. She works in a care setting with irregular breaks and frequent patient transfers. Over recent months she describes cumulative fatigue, with perceived worsening of seizure control coinciding with longer shifts and disrupted sleep.

Following the recent medication adjustment, focal impaired-awareness seizures have been occurring more often, two to four times per week, whereas previously they only happened once or twice a month. She and her employer report missed cues at work and brief post-ictal confusion. She has not had any generalised tonic–clonic seizures since June but notes more frequent prodromal symptoms (sudden blankness, oral automatisms) during busy evening rounds. There have been no injuries, though she feels less confident performing manual handling tasks and has requested more consistent break scheduling.

She reports full adherence to prescribed medication and denies intercurrent illness or alcohol use. No new triggers identified beyond fatigue and irregular meals. There has been no recent requirement for emergency rescue therapy. Neurological examination in clinic today was unchanged. 

Given the above, I am concerned that her overall condition is deteriorating, with increased seizure burden impacting occupational function. We discussed workplace adjustments and the importance of regular rest periods and hydration; she will explore options with her line manager. I have arranged an expedited review, seizure diary monitoring, and liaison with our epilepsy specialist nurse for safety planning at work. Bloods for therapeutic drug monitoring and routine biochemistry were taken today; we will contact her with results.

I will see Laura Bennett again in 6–8 weeks or sooner if there is any further deterioration.

Yours sincerely

KINGS NEUROSCIENCES CENTRE

Clinic Date: 28 September 2016

Dr Wang
Saffron Park Hospital

Saffron Park, London, E14 7JL
Dear Dr Wang
John Doe, DOB: 21-11-1982, Hospital No: P546484 NHS No. 5484656746
Flat 15 Roundwood Road, London, E14 7JL

Thank you for asking me to review your patient in the Neurology Clinic. He is known to have generalised epilepsy and remains under long-term antiseizure therapy with bone-health monitoring recorded elsewhere in his notes. I last reviewed him three months ago when we simplified his regimen to improve daytime alertness and reduce cumulative adverse effects.

Since that visit, there has been a marked change in his day-to-day seizure pattern. Following the recent medication adjustment, focal impaired-awareness seizures have been occurring more often, three - four times per day, whereas previously they only happened once or twice a month. He describes brief episodes of behavioural arrest with staring, loss of awareness and post-event confusion lasting 5–10 minutes, occasionally followed by headache. There have been no generalised tonic–clonic seizures reported over the past six weeks. He denies new injuries, tongue biting or incontinence. Triggers noted include sleep deprivation and missed meals; alcohol intake is minimal. Family members have recorded typical events on a smartphone, which corroborate the semiology and frequency he reports.

Current medicines (patient-reported): lamotrigine 200 mg b.d. and levetiracetam 1 g b.d. The adjustment three months ago involved tapering and discontinuation of topiramate over four weeks. He reports improved clarity of thinking since then, but the increase in focal impaired-awareness events started soon after the taper. No rash, mood instability or gastrointestinal intolerance reported. He drives neither a car nor a motorcycle.

Examination today is unremarkable with normal cardiorespiratory and focused neurological assessment. Observations are stable. Recent routine bloods from primary care, including FBC, U&Es and LFTs, are within reference limits as per shared results. Bone-health surveillance and vitamin D monitoring are documented in his long-term therapy record held elsewhere.

Plan discussed with the patient:
- Diagnostic clarification: although he is known to have generalised epilepsy, the current increase in focal impaired-awareness episodes following the medication change warrants repeat EEG with hyperventilation and photic stimulation, and consideration of ambulatory EEG to assess interictal generalised discharges versus focal onset features.
- Safety: reinforced seizure first-aid and avoidance of heights, open water and unsupervised bathing. Driving advice unchanged (not driving).
- Medications: no emergent adverse effects reported; we agreed not to make further changes today pending EEG and review of smartphone event videos in clinic.
- Follow-up: clinic review in 6–8 weeks, earlier if events escalate or if a generalised tonic–clonic seizure occurs.

I will update you once the EEG has been completed and we have reviewed the recordings with him. Please let me know if there is any additional information from primary care or if issues arise before his next appointment.

Yours sincerely

Epilepsy Centre 

Neurosciences Division 

Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 

Dr Patel  
St Thomas' Hospital  
Neurosciences Department, Westminster Bridge Road, London SE1 7EH  

Dear Dr Patel,  

Emily Dawson, DOB: 14-11-1990, Hospital No: R928417 NHS No. 7401563928  
58 Alder Grove, London, SW8 1JP  

Diagnoses: 

Symptomatic generalised epilepsy. 

I reviewed Emily Dawson in clinic today. She attends alone and reports a notable deterioration in her seizure control over the past 4–5 months. Historically, she has generalised epilepsy and she has a past history of atonic seizures, drop attacks and generalised tonic–clonic seizures one to two times per year, but seizure control has been excellent, and she has now been seizure free for several years. However, since increasing work pressures and longer hours, she has experienced clusters of jumps almost daily, particularly on workdays, consistent with her report that high workload has been a precipitating factor. She describes these as brief, sudden axial and upper limb jerks with occasional object dropping; she also notes intermittent disequilibrium and near‑falls. There have been two definite drop events in the last six weeks. No generalised tonic–clonic seizures have been witnessed, but her partner reports brief staring and word‑finding pauses on two occasions. 

She links the worsening to work‑related stress and poor sleep. Events tend to cluster on workdays per patient report, with relative improvement on weekends. There is no recent intercurrent illness, alcohol excess, or new medications. She denies missed anti‑seizure medication, though acknowledges variable timing on late shifts. Menses regular; no pregnancy. 

Current treatment: lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily; levetiracetam 1,000 mg twice daily. She has tolerated these without rash or mood lability; mild irritability attributed to work fatigue. She is not using rescue medication currently. No vagus nerve stimulator in situ. 

Examination today was unremarkable: alert, oriented, speech fluent; cranial nerves intact; no focal motor deficit; gait steady in clinic though she describes occasional morning unsteadiness. Blood pressure 118/72, pulse 72 regular. 

Given the deterioration and daily clustering of myoclonic‑type events, I have discussed seizure safety at work (avoidance of ladders, hot surfaces; shower rather than bath; supervision with heavy machinery) and driving regulations. She does not currently drive. We agreed to obtain updated bloods (U&Es, LFTs, FBC, vitamin D) and anti‑seizure medication levels where available, and to arrange an EEG, including activation procedures, to look for generalised spike‑wave or polyspike‑wave activity. A brain MRI from 2018 was normal; we will repeat MRI if clinically indicated after EEG review. 

She will start a structured sleep routine and stress‑reduction plan (patient‑led), and keep a seizure diary noting triggers, timing, and any clusters. We also discussed the option of dose optimisation if events persist; plan to consider a cautious lamotrigine uptitration or adjunctive valproate discussion if appropriate and acceptable in future. She understands this is an interim plan while we complete investigations. 

In summary, despite several years of excellent control, there is clear worsening temporally associated with occupational stress: she has experienced clusters of jumps almost daily, with occasional drops and brief absences suggested. This represents a deterioration from her prior baseline of rare events. I have asked her to contact the service urgently if she has any generalised tonic–clonic seizures, injuries, or any prolonged clusters. 

Follow‑up in 6–8 weeks after EEG, or sooner if needed. 

Yours sincerely

Sarah Whitfield, DOB: 22-03-1992, Hospital No: K839204 NHS No. 1029384756  
Flat 4, 11 Brook Lane, Surbiton, KT6 5AJ  

Diagnosis: 

Generalised epilepsy with ongoing generalised myoclonic and absence seizures; deterioration in control with frequent clusters following recent minor head injury 

Aetiology: 

Presumed idiopathic generalised epilepsy phenotype; recent exacerbation temporally related to minor head trauma (fall on pavement, no loss of consciousness) 

Other Medical Problems: 

Migraine without aura (intermittent), vitamin D insufficiency on supplementation, mild generalised anxiety symptoms related to seizure unpredictability 

Management Plan: 

- Increase Levetiracetam to 1,500 mg twice daily; advise consistent single-brand supply.  
- Commence Sodium Valproate modified release 250 mg nocte for one week, then 500 mg nocte if tolerated; discuss contraception and pregnancy prevention measures in detail and provide written information.  
- Provide urgent referral to physiotherapy for falls risk assessment and provision of home safety advice.  
- Arrange ambulatory EEG and serum antiepileptic drug levels in 2 weeks; repeat bone profile and vitamin D.  
- Safety counselling given regarding bathing, cooking with hot oil, and height hazards; advise not to drive and to follow DVLA guidance.  
- Review in 6 weeks, earlier if further injuries or escalation of clusters occur. 

Clinical Summary: 

Since her last routine review, there has been a clear deterioration in seizure control with events now associated with falls and minor injuries (bruising to knees and right forearm Ã‚Â· small superficial abrasion). The patient reports that these episodes are predominantly early morning and upon fatigue. Since the head injury, she has experienced clusters of jumps almost 1 per day, which she and her partner recognise as generalised myoclonic jerks sometimes preceded by a brief blank spell. She also describes brief staring episodes with rapid recovery, occurring several times per week, consistent with absence seizures. There is no focal onset history, tongue biting is rare, and there has been no status epilepticus. 

Medication adherence has been generally good; however, she reports intermittent missed evening doses during periods of stress ï¿½ we discussed strategies including alarms and a pillbox. Levetiracetam at 1,000 mg twice daily is no longer sufficient, and a cautious up-titration is planned. Given the pattern of generalised epilepsy and the myoclonic clusters, we discussed introducing Sodium Valproate, acknowledging its efficacy for generalised epilepsies. We reviewed reproductive risks in detail, provided the Patient Guide, and confirmed she is on reliable contraception. Alternatives (Lamotrigine, Topiramate) were discussed; patient preference is to trial Valproate given previous partial response to Levetiracetam and escalating injuries. 

On examination today, she was alert and oriented, with no focal neurological deficit. Gait steady between myoclonic bursts; mild tenderness over right forearm abrasion. Blood pressure 116/72, pulse 74, BMI 22.1. No signs of infection or metabolic precipitants. 

Red flags for deterioration were explained, including prolonged clusters, new head trauma, or any event lasting over 5 minutes â€ or repeated events without recovery; she and her partner have an emergency plan and contact numbers. We also provided a personalised seizure diary (paper and app options) to document timing, triggers, and injuries. 

Given the increase in frequency and the occurrence of falls, I consider her current state to be a deterioration that warrants the above medication changes, expedited investigations, and enhanced safety measures. 

Yours sincerely

National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery 

Clinic Date: 12 September 2025 

Dr Patel  
Hillside Medical Practice  
14 Brook Street, London W1D 3QS  

Dear Dr Patel,  

Emily Carter, DOB: 22-07-1991, Hospital No: U928374 NHS No. 1029384756  
Flat 4, 28 Rosebank Avenue, London N12 8QP 

Summary/ Diagnoses: History of seizures with cognitive complaints/low mood symptoms under primary care review/migraine without aura/GERD/exercise‑induced asthma. 

Medication: Lamotrigine 100 mg twice daily.  
Clonazepam 0.5 mg at night as needed for sleep (patient reports infrequent use).  
Omeprazole 20 mg daily.  
Salbutamol inhaler as required.  
Sumatriptan 50 mg as needed for migraine (maximum two doses per attack).  

I reviewed Emily Carter in clinic today, accompanied by her partner who has kept a symptom diary since June. She reports increased daytime lapses in attention and brief speech arrest episodes, particularly on workdays with higher cognitive load. Sleep has been fragmented due to early shifts; alcohol intake is minimal (1–2 units/week). No new head injuries. She continues to work part‑time in retail and is currently not driving. Neurologically, examination today was non‑focal. BP 118/72 mmHg, pulse 72 bpm regular. No tremor. Gait normal. 

Seizures: Since our last review in May, the patient notes a clear increase in brief staring spells with unresponsiveness lasting 5–15 seconds, occasionally followed by a few minutes of fatigue without confusion. His absence seizures are now occurring on two to three days of the week, whereas previously they were restricted to once every couple of weeks. The diary suggests clustering after poor sleep and during periods of stress. No reported generalised convulsions, tongue biting, significant injury, or incontinence. Partner‑witnessed events corroborate the frequency change. 

Investigations: EEG (July 2025) showed intermittent generalised spike‑and‑wave activity during hyperventilation without photoparoxysmal response. MRI brain (August 2025) unremarkable. Routine bloods from GP (August 2025): FBC, U&E, LFTs, B12, folate, TSH within reference; vitamin D borderline low at 23 nmol/L. 

Plan:  
- Increase lamotrigine to 125 mg twice daily for two weeks, then 150 mg twice daily if tolerated; counselled regarding rash and to seek urgent review if this occurs.  
- Issue rescue plan: if clusters exceed usual pattern, contact epilepsy specialist nurse for same‑week review.  
- Sleep hygiene advice reinforced; avoid sleep deprivation and consider adjusting early shifts if feasible.  
- Start vitamin D3 1000 IU daily via OTC to address low level; recheck in 3 months via GP.  
- Provide updated seizure diary template to capture potential triggers and recovery time.  
- DVLA guidance discussed; patient already not driving and will continue to refrain pending stability as per national guidance.  
- Follow‑up in 12 weeks with interim phone check by epilepsy nurse in 4 weeks, sooner if further increase in frequency or any new prolonged episodes.  

Yours sincerely

With best wishes,

Clinic Date: 21 September 2025 

Dr Hannah Patel  
St George’s University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust  
Atkinson Morley Wing, Blackshaw Road, London SW17 0QT  

Dear Dr Hannah Patel,  

Mr Daniel Reeves, DOB: 14-02-1990, Hospital No: H392774 NHS No. 9034271562  
Flat 3, 12 Willow Grove, Mitcham, CR4 2NH 

Diagnoses: 

Primary generalised epilepsy with absence seizures  
EEG (May 2024): Generalised spike-and-wave discharges consistent with generalised epilepsy 

Current Medication: 

Sodium Valproate 500 mg bd  
Clobazam 10 mg nocte (intermittent use for clusters) 

Plan: 

- Continue Sodium Valproate 500 mg twice daily  
- Maintain seizure diary capturing work conditions (heat exposure, duration of exertion)  
- Liaise with Occupational Health regarding heat mitigation and rest breaks outdoors  
- Routine review in 4 months, earlier if further deterioration or safety concerns 

I reviewed Mr Daniel Reeves in clinic today. He works in gardening/groundskeeping outdoors, and he reports that heat and prolonged exertion vary seasonally. Over the last three months, he has noticed a clear increase in brief lapses of awareness while working in warmer conditions and during longer tasks. His absence seizures are now occurring on two - three days of the week, whereas previously they were restricted to once every couple of months. Episodes last 5–10 seconds without falls, tongue biting, or incontinence, but he occasionally needs to pause tasks and has twice misplaced tools during a lapse. There have been no generalised tonic–clonic seizures and no myoclonic jerks reported. Sleep is generally adequate; alcohol minimal; no recent intercurrent illness. 

He remains adherent to Sodium Valproate 500 mg twice daily. He uses Clobazam 10 mg at night intermittently when he anticipates clusters; he reports mild morning grogginess but no other adverse effects. He has begun recording ambient temperature and workload in his seizure diary, which may help clarify a seasonal/environmental pattern. We discussed practical, non-prescriptive strategies he has tried at work (seeking shade when available, pacing tasks), which he feels help modestly. 

Neurological examination today was unremarkable. Given that this is primary generalised epilepsy with current absence predominance and a recent increase in frequency, I have recommended continuing his current antiepileptic regimen unchanged for now while we gather more structured diary data and liaise with Occupational Health regarding feasible adjustments to outdoor duties. If the pattern persists despite environmental measures, we will consider dose optimisation or an alternative adjunct at review. He is aware of DVLA guidance and confirms no driving. 

Yours sincerely,

Flat 3, 28 Highgate Road, London, NW5 1NR  

Focal Epilepsy

Transition to Adult Services: This was Daniel Hughes’s first review in the adult neurology clinic following transition from paediatric services. His mother attended and provided collateral history with his consent. We discussed ongoing management, self-management skills, and plans for shared decision-making as he settles into adult care.

Epilepsy Type: The history is consistent with focal epilepsy, with focal impaired awareness episodes characterised by brief behavioural arrest, vacant expression, and subtle right-hand automatisms lasting 15–30 seconds, followed by mild post-event confusion.

Seizures: His absence seizures are now occurring on three days of the week, whereas previously they were restricted to once every couple of weeks. He and his mother report that events cluster towards late afternoon on school days, with occasional brief myoclonic jerks on awakening but no generalised convulsions. There is no tongue biting, injury or incontinence reported.

Medication: Currently on Levetiracetam 750 mg twice daily since February 2025 (converted from Oxcarbazepine due to mood-related adverse effects). He uses Buccal Midazolam 5 mg as a rescue plan only if any event exceeds 3 minutes (not required to date). No other regular medications.

Adherence and Tolerability: He reports good adherence using a phone reminder app. Mild irritability noted in the first month of Levetiracetam initiation has settled; no current mood or sleep concerns.

Triggers and Lifestyle: He notes poorer sleep during exam periods and skipped lunches on busy college days. No alcohol or recreational drug use reported. He is starting driving lessons planning for the future; we reviewed DVLA guidance regarding seizure freedom requirements.

Investigations and Prior Results: Childhood MRI (age 12) reported as normal. Paediatric EEG (age 15) showed left temporal interictal spikes. No adult EEG completed since transition; we discussed updating EEG to reassess current interictal activity. Bloods (July 2025) normal FBC/U&Es/LFTs; Vitamin D borderline low (48 nmol/L) and he is taking over-the-counter supplementation per GP advice.

Safety and Support: Seizure first-aid and risk minimisation reviewed, including showering rather than bathing unsupervised, and kitchen safety precautions. His mother remains an emergency contact and will continue to attend when possible to provide collateral information.

Plan Agreed Today:
- Continue Levetiracetam 750 mg twice daily without change pending updated assessment.
- Arrange routine EEG and consider ambulatory EEG if interictal yield is low but clinical suspicion remains high.
- Maintain seizure diary capturing time of day, precipitating factors, and recovery profile.
- Optimise sleep hygiene and regular meals; college letter offered to support adjustments during assessments.
- DVLA advice reiterated; not currently driving. Will revisit once seizure control improves and statutory requirements are met.
- Telephone review in 8 weeks to reassess frequency and discuss results, with in-person follow-up in 4–6 months or sooner if deterioration occurs.

Yours sincerely

King's College Hospital 

Department of Neurosciences 

Clinic Date: 10 June 2017 

Dr Priya Nair
Consultant Neurologist  
King's College Hospital  
Department of Neurosciences, King's College Hospital, London SE5 9RS  

Dear Dr Priya Nair
Consultant Neurologist,  

James Carter, DOB: 15-03-1990, Hospital No: KCH872991 NHS No. 9076543211  
Flat 3, 12 Brook Lane, London, SE15 2HT

Thank you for asking me to review your patient. He attended with his long‑term carer, who assists with day‑to‑day communication and maintains a seizure diary. The carer reports a clear recent change in the pattern of events recorded. Over the past few months, tonic seizures have increased in frequency to two to three per week, in contrast to the earlier pattern of one seizure every month or two. These are typically brief, with sudden stiffening, a grunt, and a fall risk if standing, followed by confusion and fatigue lasting 20–40 minutes. There is no consistent aura reported. Injuries have included minor forearm bruising and one lip bite; there have been no head injuries.

The carer notes that episodes tend to cluster in the late evening. Potential precipitating factors described include poor sleep and missed meals on days with changes to routine. No clear association with intercurrent illness, alcohol, or new over‑the‑counter medicines has been identified. There are occasional nocturnal events suggested by bed disarray and morning confusion, but no witnessed nocturnal generalised convulsions have been logged.

Communication in clinic was facilitated by simple, direct questions and visual prompts. He was calm, cooperative, and engaged with support. There were no focal neurological deficits on examination. Cardiovascular and general examination were unremarkable. The seizure diary maintained by the carer appears internally consistent and spans the past 9 months with daily entries.

Current medicines as reported by the carer: levetiracetam 1 g twice daily, lamotrigine 200 mg twice daily, and midazolam 10 mg buccal for prolonged events (not used in the past 6 months). There have been no recent dose changes. No drug allergies are known. He lives in supported accommodation with staff present 24/7. A personalised safety plan is in place, including supervised bathing and environmental adjustments to reduce fall hazards.

Given the reported escalation in events and the absence of clear triggers on history, I have requested an updated routine EEG and will arrange ambulatory monitoring if the initial study is non‑informative. I have also asked for serum levels of current antiseizure medications, renal and hepatic profiles, vitamin D, and a repeat full blood count. We will coordinate with the community learning disability team to ensure reasonable adjustments for investigations and to provide accessible appointment information. The carer is willing to continue detailed logging, including time of day, context, potential triggers, and recovery features.

I discussed emergency thresholds in accessible language with the patient and carer, and confirmed they know how to access urgent support should events change in character or duration. A follow‑up appointment has been booked in 8–10 weeks, or earlier if the frequency escalates further or new features emerge.

Thank you for your ongoing care. Please let me know if there are additional aspects you would like us to address at the next review.

Yours sincerely

Epilepsy Centre 

Neurosciences Division 

Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 

Dr Emily Carter  
St. Thomas' Hospital  
Westminster Bridge Road, London SE1 7EH  

Dear Dr Emily Carter,  

Laura Bennett, DOB: 14-02-1991, Hospital No: A9374621 NHS No. 9081726453  
12 Brookside Close, Croydon, CR0 5HL  

Diagnoses: 

Seizure disorder under investigation. 

Thank you for asking me to review Laura Bennett in clinic. She attended today alone. She is the primary caregiver for two young children, and reports that night-time sleep is frequently interrupted due to childcare needs. Over the past few months, tonic seizures have increased in frequency to seven per week, in contrast to the earlier pattern of one seizure every month or two. These episodes are described as sudden stiffening with brief unresponsiveness lasting 15–30 seconds, most often occurring in the early morning hours and occasionally around sleep onset. There is no clear precipitant identified beyond sleep disruption; she denies alcohol use and has been avoiding missed doses of medication. She reports occasional tongue biting but no major injuries or prolonged post-ictal confusion. There is no reliable aura. 

Current medications: 
- Levetiracetam 1,000 mg twice daily.  
- Vitamin D 1,000 IU daily. 

Adherence is self-reported as good and pharmacy records corroborate timely refills. She notes increased irritability since dose escalation of levetiracetam in June, but no rash or systemic symptoms. No rescue medication has been required and there have been no emergency department presentations. 

Investigations and monitoring: 
- EEG (July 2025): intermittent generalised and focal-appearing sharp transients without clear localisation; not definitively lateralising.  
- MRI brain (August 2025): structurally normal study.  
- Routine bloods (September 2025): FBC, U&E, LFTs within reference limits. 

Assessment: 

There has been a clinically significant increase in seizure frequency temporally associated with ongoing sleep fragmentation due to caregiving responsibilities. While imaging is unremarkable, the EEG is non-specific. Tolerability to current therapy is borderline due to mood irritability. Driving status and safety around heights, bathing, and infant handling were discussed; she confirms she is not currently driving. We reviewed seizure first aid and strategies to improve sleep opportunity where feasible. 

Plan: 
1) Optimise antiseizure therapy: introduce lamotrigine with slow titration while maintaining levetiracetam for now; consider later cross-taper if mood effects persist.  
   - Lamotrigine: start 25 mg once daily for 2 weeks, then 25 mg twice daily for 2 weeks, then increase by 25–50 mg every 1–2 weeks towards 100–150 mg twice daily as tolerated. Education given regarding rash and need to seek urgent review if it develops.

- I will arrange a rapid-access telephone review in four weeks and refer to our epilepsy nurse specialist for coaching on aura-response strategies and injury prevention.

I spoke with Amelia Hart today in clinic. She is motivated, understands her focal epilepsy diagnosis, and is confident using her established aura recognition strategies; she requests written information for her workplace, which I will provide.

Yours sincerely

St Mary's Hospital 

Institute of Neurology 

Clinic Date: 24 May 2017 

Dr Ahmed  
St Mary's Hospital  
Institute of Neurology, St Mary's Hospital, London W2 1NY  

Dear Dr Ahmed,  

Daniel Morris, DOB: 12-11-1982, Hospital No: H594203 NHS No. 5839201746  
14 Brookside Close, London, W10 6AB 

Medication:  

Levetiracetam 1000 mg twice daily. Patient-reported good adherence; no significant adverse effects beyond mild irritability in the evenings. Naproxen 500 mg as needed for migraine; uses approximately twice per month with fair benefit. 

Thank you for asking me to review him in clinic today with ongoing episodes suggestive of seizures, on a background of intermittent migraine without aura. The current clinical focus is epilepsy management, while noting his migraine history which has remained stable and is not the primary driver of today’s assessment. 

Since his last appointment, the patient and his partner have kept a diary of events. In March he had 3 in sleep and 2 while awake. In May he had 3 in sleep and 3 while awake. These were brief, self-terminating, and without clear provocation. No clear diurnal pattern beyond the nocturnal clustering was identified. He describes a subjective sense of internal "rush" and occasional metallic taste immediately beforehand, but there has been no tongue-biting, no prolonged post-event confusion, and no injury. He denies alcohol excess; sleep has been variable due to shift work. 

He underwent routine bloods locally which were within reference limits (U&E, LFT, FBC). MRI brain from last year was reported as structurally unremarkable. A routine EEG performed previously was non-diagnostic. We discussed the potential value of ambulatory EEG if events persist at similar frequency; he is content to consider this. 

We have not altered his antiseizure medication today. I advised continued diary-keeping, attention to sleep hygiene, and to continue migraine measures as currently used, noting that naproxen has not coincided with any change in event frequency. He will also trial a consistent pre-sleep routine for four weeks to reduce nocturnal variability. No driving reported; I reiterated standard safety precautions at home (showers rather than baths, avoid heights, and cooking with care). 

If the nocturnal episodes continue at the current rate over the next 6–8 weeks or if any event lasts longer than five minutes or clusters without recovery, he should seek urgent review. Otherwise, we will see him back in three months. 

Please let me know if there are any concerns in the interim. 

Yours sincerely

University College Hospital 

National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery 

Clinic Date: 29 December 2021 

Dr Susan  
University College Hospital  
National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery, London WC1N 3BG  

Dear Dr Susan,  

Emily Carter, DOB: 22-07-1988, Hospital No: E748521 NHS No. 1064938275  
Flat 12, 4 Kingfisher Court, London, NW1 5QE 

Summary/ Diagnoses: Generalised epilepsy with recent deterioration in seizure control; probable medication non-adherence secondary to delayed access to rescue medication and refills due to cleanroom/data-hall workplace restrictions; migraine without aura; vitamin D insufficiency; mild GORD; non-smoker; no current alcohol use. 

Medication: Sodium Valproate (Depakote) 500 mg twice daily.  
Lamotrigine 150 mg morning and 200 mg evening.  
Clobazam 10 mg at night (recently increased from 5 mg in October 2021).  
Midazolam 10 mg buccal solution as rescue, to be used for seizures >5 minutes or clusters.  
Omeprazole 20 mg once daily.  
Vitamin D3 1000 IU once daily.  

Previous antiepileptic therapies: Levetiracetam (stopped due to mood irritability); Topiramate (stopped due to cognitive slowing and paraesthesiae). 

I reviewed Emily Carter in clinic today. She attended alone. She works in a controlled cleanroom/data-hall environment with strict badge access and tool-down protocols. She reports that retrieval of rescue medication and obtaining on-time refills are often significantly delayed because her medication cannot be brought into the hall and release from station requires supervisor clearance. As a result, she has missed several doses over the last two months and has noticed a clear worsening of seizure control. She describes increased daytime fatigue, post-ictal confusion lasting up to an hour, and new tongue-biting on two occasions. There have been no reported injuries or head strikes, but she has had two near-falls at work. 

Seizures: She has generalised epilepsy with typical events comprising abrupt loss of awareness with generalised tonic-clonic activity, lateral tongue-bite, and post-ictal confusion. There are also occasional myoclonic jerks in the mornings when sleep-deprived. She kept a brief calendar record for November and December. In Nov she had four seizures during sleep and 3 while awake. In December she had one in sleep and five while awake. These figures represent a significant deterioration compared with earlier in the year when she had gone several months with only rare myoclonic jerks and no convulsions. There is a clear temporal association between missed or delayed doses and seizure occurrence, particularly on late shifts when access to her medication locker is restricted. 

Examination: Pulse 72 bpm regular, BP 118/72 mmHg. Neurological examination normal between events. No focal deficits. Gait steady. 

Investigations: Previous MRI brain (2019) normal. Prior routine EEG (2019) showed generalised spike-and-wave discharges consistent with generalised epilepsy. No recent bloods available today. 

Impression: Generalised epilepsy with clinically significant deterioration in seizure control coinciding with workplace-related delays in rescue medication and refill access leading to missed doses. Risk heightened by shift pattern and environmental constraints. 

Plan: 
- Epilepsy medication: Increase Clobazam to 10 mg twice daily as interim measure pending review of adherence solutions and monitoring for sedation. Continue Sodium Valproate 500 mg twice daily and Lamotrigine 150 mg morning/200 mg evening. 
- Rescue medication: Provide duplicate Midazolam 10 mg buccal packs—one retained with Occupational Health outside the cleanroom and one in a personal grab-bag at the security desk to minimise retrieval delays. 
- Occupational adjustments: Letter to employer/Occupational Health requesting a reasonable adjustment to allow timed exit for medication dosing and secure storage at access control; designate trained first-aiders for rescue administration. 
- Safety: Seizure first-aid advice reiterated; avoid lone working on night shifts; consider temporary restriction from high-risk tasks until control improves. 
- Monitoring: Check U&Es, LFTs, FBC, vitamin D level, and valproate level; lamotrigine level if available. Arrange 24-hour ambulatory EEG if further breakthrough events despite improved access. 
- Follow-up: Nurse-led phone review in 4 weeks to assess response and adherence; consultant review in 3 months or sooner if seizures cluster or injuries occur. 

Yours sincerely

Epilepsy Centre

Neurosciences Division

From: Dr Alice Morgan (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST)
Date: 13 January 2024
To: neurology.team@nhs.net
Cc: Dr John Williams (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST); Dr Sarah Patel (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST)
Subject: Review and update

Dear Alice,

Diagnosis overview:
The working classification of seizures remains under review.

Current medication:
1. Carbamazepine (modified release) 600 mg twice daily
2. Levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily

Recent course and seizure description:
Since our last contact, the patient has implemented light and screen management strategies (reduced evening screen exposure, blue‑light filtering, and regular sleep timing). He reports feeling more stable and believes these changes have contributed to improvement. Specifically, the recent pattern has been as follows: In October he had two seizures during sleep and none while awake. In December he had three in sleep and no while awake. No clear daytime precipitants have been identified, and there have been no injuries, tongue bites, or prolonged post‑ictal confusional states. Mood and energy are reported as better overall, with fewer interrupted nights.

Assessment:
On balance he perceives improvement, particularly with respect to daytime functioning and reduced concern about wakeful episodes. There is no evidence of new adverse effects from current medication. Light/screen management appears to be a helpful component of his routine.

Plan:
- Continue current doses of carbamazepine (modified release) and levetiracetam unchanged for now.
- Maintain the light and screen hygiene measures (blue‑light filters after sunset, regular bedtime, breaks from screens in the evening), which he feels are beneficial.
- Keep a seizure and sleep diary noting timing (sleep vs wake), potential triggers, and recovery times.
- Safety advice reinforced regarding nocturnal events (use of padded bed edges where appropriate, and sleeping position guidance as discussed).
- Follow‑up in four months; sooner if events change in character, occur when awake, or cluster.

Please let me know if there are any concerns before the next review.

With best wishes,

Epilepsy Centre

Neurosciences Division

Clinic Date: 25 July 2014

Dr Patel
St George’s University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
Blackshaw Road, London SW17 0QT

Dear Dr Patel,

Michael Brown, DOB: 14-02-1987, Hospital No: H482917 NHS No. 9075312468
12 Brookside Close, London, SW12 8DA

Diagnoses:

Seizure disorder under investigation.

Thank you for reviewing Michael Brown, who attended today with his partner. He works rotating shifts, including nights, and both he and his partner report that his circadian rhythm has been disrupted for several months due to frequent changes in start times. He has noticed that sleep deprivation after night shifts often precedes events.

Since his last review he has not required emergency medication and there have been no injuries or prolonged events. In Jun he had a nocturnal seizure but no daytime events. In July he had three nocturnal seizures and 5 while awake. He and his partner kept a diary that correlates the nocturnal events with sequences of two or more late finishes, and the daytime events with early-morning starts following short sleep. There have been no clear focal warnings reported, and no consistent postictal confusion beyond brief fatigue. He denies alcohol or recreational drug use and has maintained regular meals despite the schedule.

Current medications are unchanged from the last visit. He has not used any rescue therapy in this interval. There is no implanted device in situ and no previous neurosurgical intervention. He is using a smartphone alarm to prompt regular dosing and has started a sleep hygiene plan (patient-led) aimed at stabilising bedtime on non-working days.

On examination today he was well, with normal cardiorespiratory and neurological examination between events. We reiterated the importance of maintaining a seizure diary with precise timing relative to shift patterns. He will continue with the current regimen while we complete further diagnostics already arranged (including repeat EEG with sleep deprivation and serum levels, as discussed previously). We also provided written information on occupational safety around night work, which he and his employer can review.

We will plan a follow-up in three months, or sooner if there is any escalation in frequency, injuries, or events lasting longer than usual. He and his partner are aware of red flags and how to contact the service.

Yours sincerely

Epilepsy Centre

Neurosciences Division


From: Dr Emily Carter (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST)
Sent: 13 June 2025 10:20
To: kch-epilepsy@nhs.net
Cc: Dr Ravi Desai (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST); Dr Hannah O’Neill (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST)
Subject: Post-partum deterioration and treatment adjustment

Hi Emily

Epilepsy Diagnosis:

Focal epilepsy, probable temporal lobe onset, with secondary generalisation reported on two occasions historically. Patient has focal epilepsy.

Present Medication:

1. Lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily
2. Levetiracetam 750 mg twice daily

Present Seizure Frequency:

Since delivery six months ago, the patient reports a perceived worsening of seizures alongside low mood and marked fatigue. In Mar she had five seizures during sleep and 5 while awake. In May she had no in sleep and one while awake. Her partner corroborates that nocturnal events in March included automatisms and post-ictal confusion on waking, while the daytime events were brief focal impaired-awareness episodes with lip smacking and speech arrest, one progressing to a bilateral tonic–clonic seizure.

Plan of Action:

The clinical picture suggests post-partum deterioration, likely influenced by sleep deprivation and mood symptoms. Despite therapeutic lamotrigine levels checked last month, breakthrough focal seizures persist. To address this:
- Increase lamotrigine to 200 mg twice daily over two weeks (increase by 25–50 mg per dose every 5–7 days as tolerated), monitoring for rash or dizziness.
- Continue levetiracetam 750 mg twice daily unchanged for now. The patient reports irritability and low mood post-partum; we discussed that levetiracetam can exacerbate mood symptoms. If mood remains problematic after lamotrigine optimisation, we will consider tapering levetiracetam and switching to brivaracetam.
- Safety: reinforce seizure first aid, no driving as per DVLA guidance following recent events, and avoid unsupervised bathing/co-sleeping with the infant.
- Support: referral to perinatal mental health team for assessment of low mood and fatigue; advise sleep hygiene strategies and partner-supported night feeds where possible.
- Investigations: arrange repeat EEG with sleep deprivation and an updated MRI epilepsy protocol (last imaging 2019). Check lamotrigine trough level in four weeks after dose escalation.
- Follow-up: review in clinic in 8–10 weeks. Earlier review if seizure frequency increases, adverse effects occur, or mood deteriorates further.

Overall, the condition is currently deteriorating in the post-partum period by patient and partner report, though May shows partial improvement; we will prioritise seizure control while addressing mood and sleep contributors.

With best wishes

Centre for Epilepsy

Neurosciences Division

Clinic Date: 4 February 2021

Dr A Sharma
Consultant Neurologist
Centre for Epilepsy
King’s College Hospital, Denmark Hill, London SE5 9RS

Dear Dr A Sharma,

Ms Emma Carter, DOB: 22-07-1992, Hospital No: K842917 NHS No. 9384756201
Flat 3, 25 Brook Lane, London, SE15 4AB

Diagnosis:

Generalised epilepsy with nocturnal and occasional daytime events; good response to Sodium Valproate, partial response to Levetiracetam previously; Lamotrigine avoided due to patient-reported mood effects.

Aetiology:

Unclear; no focal neurological deficits. Family history negative for epilepsy. Normal MRI brain (2019). EEG (2020) showed generalised spike–wave discharges.

Other Medical Problems:

Post-partum within the last six months; night-time sleep fragmented. Iron deficiency anaemia on oral supplementation.

Management Plan:

- Continue Sodium Valproate 500 mg mane and 1000 mg nocte; maintain single manufacturer brand.
- Optimise sleep where possible given infant care; patient to trial shared night feeds three nights per week to reduce sleep fragmentation.
- Seizure safety reviewed, including bathing supervision and driving advice (not driving; will reassess per DVLA guidance after seizure-free interval).
- Bloods in 8 weeks: valproate level, FBC, LFTs.
- Follow-up in three months by video; earlier review if events cluster or daytime seizures increase.

History and Current Status:

She is six months post-partum and reports substantially broken sleep related to infant care. Against this background, she described the following pattern: In Nov he had 3 seizures during sleep and 1 while awake. In Jan he had five in sleep and one while awake. These events were witnessed by her partner as brief generalised convulsions from sleep with tongue biting and myalgia afterwards; the daytime events were shorter, with transient loss of awareness and brief bilateral shaking. No injuries reported. Medication adherence has been good, and there have been no intercurrent illnesses. She notices events cluster after multiple consecutive nights of <4 hours’ continuous sleep.

Examination (telemedicine):

Alert, oriented, no focal signs reported. No rash or tremor observed on video.

Summary:

This patient has generalised epilepsy with recent breakthrough seizures temporally associated with severe sleep disruption in the post-partum period. We will continue Valproate, monitor levels and liver profile, and focus on sleep optimisation and safety. I will review in three months.

Yours sincerely

Centre for Epilepsy

Neurosciences Division

Clinic Date: 10 January 2015

Dr Martin Hale  
Centre for Epilepsy  
Queen Square, London WC1N 3BG  

Dear Dr Martin Hale,

Thomas Walker, DOB: 22-11-1984, Hospital No: H3928475 NHS No. 8459203671  
Flat 3, 27 Linton Road, London, N1 8QU

Epilepsy – Focal epilepsy

Medication: The patient remains on carbamazepine modified release 400 mg twice daily, commenced August 2014, and reports good adherence without notable adverse effects. He is not on any other anti-seizure medicines. A routine carbamazepine level will be arranged at his local phlebotomy service prior to the next review.

Seizure history and current frequency: The patient has a background of focal epilepsy with events typically starting with a déjà vu aura and epigastric rising sensation, sometimes progressing to impaired awareness with automatisms. He keeps a diary and, based on his report: In Oct he had no nocturnal seizures but 5 daytime events. In December he had two nocturnal seizures and two while awake. He relates the daytime events to work-related stress and missed meals. There have been no reported generalised tonic–clonic seizures in this period, and no injuries.

Review details: I spoke with him today via scheduled telephone follow-up. He feels overall control is improving compared with earlier in the year, and he has been avoiding alcohol and maintaining regular sleep. He has not required emergency services and there have been no medication lapses. No new neurological symptoms were described. We discussed seizure safety at work and he confirms his employer is aware of his diagnosis. Driving status has been discussed and he understands current DVLA guidance for focal seizures with impaired awareness.

Plan:
- Continue carbamazepine MR 400 mg twice daily.
- Arrange trough carbamazepine level and routine bloods (FBC, U&E, LFTs) before next appointment.
- Maintain seizure diary, particularly noting sleep, meals, and stressors.
- Telephone review in 3 months, with earlier contact if frequency increases or new features emerge.

Yours sincerely,

St Mary's Hospital 

Institute of Neurology 

Clinic Date: 25 September 2024 

Dr Ahmed  
St Mary's Hospital  
Institute of Neurology, St Mary's Hospital, London W2 1NY  

Dear Dr Ahmed,  

Sophie Williams, DOB: 14-02-1992, Hospital No: N834205 NHS No. 9182736450  
Flat 2, 10 Brookside Close, London, W10 5LR 

Medication: 

Levetiracetam 1000 mg twice daily. Tolerated without notable mood change per carer report. Vitamin D supplementation 800 IU once daily. 

I reviewed Sophie Williams in epilepsy clinic today. She has a learning disability and was accompanied by her paid carer, who assists with communication and maintains a seizure log. The carer provided the primary history, supplemented by brief responses from the patient.

She has focal epilepsy. Seizure semiology as described by the carer involves brief behavioural arrest with right upper limb clenching and head deviation to the right, sometimes progressing to impaired awareness with lip smacking; post-ictal confusion typically lasts 5–10 minutes. There have been no reported injuries. The carer noted both daytime and nocturnal events in prior months. She has had no seizures so far this month, four in August, one in July and 3 in June, with events reported from both daytime and nocturnal periods. Triggers suspected by the carer include sleep deprivation and missed meals; there has been added emphasis on consistent routines within the supported living setting.

No recent intercurrent illnesses. Sleep is reported as improved after adjusting evening support staff schedules. Appetite is stable. There have been no new neurological symptoms. The patient uses a pill organiser and carer-administered reminders; no missed doses were recorded on the log since early August.

Examination today: she was alert, engaged with prompts, and followed simple commands. Speech output limited but consistent with baseline. Cranial nerves grossly intact; no focal motor deficit appreciated. Gait steady with supervision. Observations stable.

Investigations: Prior MRI (2022) showed left mesial temporal sclerosis; routine EEG (2023) with left temporal sharp waves. No recent bloods indicating adverse effects; carer to arrange annual monitoring via primary care as per shared care plan.

Plan: 
- Continue levetiracetam 1000 mg twice daily. 
- Reinforce adherence and sleep hygiene within the supported living plan; carer to continue detailed seizure logging, including time of day, semiology, duration, and recovery. 
- Provide a written, easy-read seizure first aid guide to the care team; we have updated her seizure management plan with contact numbers. 
- Consider lamotrigine adjunct if frequency increases or if clusters recur; at present, with no seizures recorded this month, we will not make a change. 
- Safety: nocturnal supervision maintained; no current driving. 

We will review her again in four months, or sooner if the seizure frequency increases or if there is any change in pattern such as prolonged events, new injuries, or generalised tonic–clonic activity.

Yours sincerely

Centre for Epilepsy

Neurosciences Division 

Clinic Date: 24 September 2011 

Dr Helen Carter  
Centre for Epilepsy  
Queen Square, London WC1N 3BG  

Dear Dr Helen Carter,                                                                                                         

Mr Daniel Fraser, DOB: 21-11-1985, Hospital No: H3928471 NHS No. 9843201765  
Flat 3, 27 Aldgate High Street, London EC3N 1AH  

Epilepsy 

Diagnosis: Generalised epilepsy (clinical history consistent with generalised onset seizures; no focal features reported).  

Medication: Ongoing Sodium Valproate since May 2011.  

Current regimen: Sodium Valproate 500 mg twice daily (enteric-coated). Patient reports full adherence, no missed doses in the past month.  

Adverse effects: Mild post-dose nausea on early shifts; no tremor, no weight change beyond baseline; no rash; no mood change reported.  

Seizure summary: He experienced 2 generalised tonic-clonic seizures so far in Sep, one in Aug, and 0 in Jul, occurring during both wakefulness and sleep. He describes a brief prodrome of light-headedness on two occasions, followed by loss of awareness and bilateral tonic–clonic activity witnessed by colleagues once on the gate line and once at home during the night. Post-ictal confusion lasts 15–30 minutes with myalgia the following day. No tongue biting reported in September; one episode of urinary incontinence in August. No known focal onset features, and no prolonged events requiring rescue medication. 

Work and safety context: He works at a busy metro station gate line where prolonged standing, variable lighting, public address announcements, and intermittent crowd surges are routine. He reports that crowd surges can make him feel overwhelmed and that dehydration is common on hot days. Colleagues have been informed of basic seizure first-aid and have assisted once without incident. He avoids working at platform edge alone when feeling unwell and takes scheduled hydration breaks when possible. 

Triggers and lifestyle: Sleep curtailment during early shifts and missed meals appear contributory. No alcohol excess; no recreational drugs. Reports adequate hydration plans now in place. 

Investigations: Prior EEG (May 2011) reportedly showed generalised spike–wave discharges (patient-reported; formal report being requested). MRI brain (April 2011) normal (patient-reported). 

Plan: 
- Continue Sodium Valproate 500 mg twice daily for now while we obtain the formal EEG/MRI reports and recent serum valproate level from the GP records.  
- Request trough Sodium Valproate level and routine bloods (FBC, LFTs) via GP.  
- Provide workplace seizure first-aid reinforcement and written guidance for his supervisor; advise continued hydration, regular meals, and sleep hygiene, particularly around early shifts.  
- Discussed safety: avoid lone duties at platform edge when unwell; ensure colleagues aware of recovery position and when to call emergency services.  
- Review in 8 weeks by telephone unless earlier if further seizures occur. 

Yours sincerely

Recurrent seizures of undetermined classification; pattern and semiology remain unclear pending further characterisation

Jane Smith, DOB: 22-03-1991, Hospital No: K847510 NHS No. 6042819753  
12 Brook Lane, London, SE1 3AB  

Diagnosis: 

Combined generalised and focal epilepsy; patient has both generalised and focal epilepsy, with prominent focal auras and occasional generalised tonic–clonic seizures. 

Aetiology: 

Unclear; MRI brain (2017) non-lesional; normal perinatal and developmental history; no family history of epilepsy. 

Other Medical Problems: 

Mild iron deficiency anaemia under GP monitoring; seasonal allergic rhinitis managed with cetirizine PRN. 

Management Plan: 

- Continue Lamotrigine 150 mg mane and 200 mg nocte, same brand.
- Continue Levetiracetam 750 mg twice daily; consider uptitration to 1000 mg twice daily if breakthrough generalised tonic–clonic events recur despite adherence and sleep optimisation.
- Buccal midazolam 10 mg as rescue for prolonged convulsive seizures >5 minutes; partner trained in administration.
- Maintain seizure diary with separate logging of focal aware auras and generalised events; record wake/sleep state and likely triggers.
- Reinforce previously learned aura recognition strategies; patient to implement pre-emptive safety steps (sit/lie down, notify partner, avoid high-risk tasks) at onset of typical warnings.
- Lifestyle: prioritise sleep regularity, hydration, and stress management; avoid alcohol excess. Driving currently not undertaken; counselled to continue to follow DVLA guidance.
- Bloods today: FBC, U&Es, LFTs, Lamotrigine and Levetiracetam trough levels to assess adherence/exposure.
- Review in 4 months or sooner if increase in convulsive frequency.

Summary of Current Status: 

She reported that her focal aware warnings remain consistent with her practiced aura recognition strategies, describing them in her own words as a “rising metallic taste, brief left-sided tingling, and a pull of attention to the right,” typically lasting under 30 seconds, occasionally progressing to impaired awareness. She noted no seizures in June, four in May, and four in April, all from mixed awake/asleep states. These were predominantly focal impaired awareness events, with one secondary generalised tonic–clonic seizure in late May following sleep deprivation. She denies injuries or prolonged postictal confusion. Medication adherence is reported as good with a single missed evening dose in April. She perceives Levetiracetam to reduce generalised events, while Lamotrigine helps with focal auras. Previous medications included Topiramate (discontinued due to cognitive slowing) and Sodium Valproate (stopped for weight gain and hair thinning; avoided due to reproductive considerations). 

Examination today was unremarkable; neurological examination normal and no focal deficits. 

I will update you after blood results are available and will adjust dosing if levels are subtherapeutic or if there is ongoing breakthrough activity despite lifestyle optimisation. 

Yours sincerely

Dr Amelia Carter

Emily Turner, DOB: 14-03-1992, Hospital No: H294771 NHS No. 9081763452  
Flat 12, 25 Jubilee Gardens, London SE1 7PB

Recurrent unprovoked seizures of uncertain classification

Levetiracetam 1000 mg bd

I will review her in 8–10 weeks after investigations. Should the frequency increase or she experiences new prolonged events, she will contact the clinic sooner via the epilepsy nurse line. 

With best wishes,

Epilepsy Centre 

Neurosciences Division

Dr Patel  
St George's University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust

Dear Dr Patel,  

Michael Harris, DOB: 14-11-1988, Hospital No: A937451 NHS No. 8420195536  
12 Brookside Close, London, SW12 8JP  

Diagnoses: 

Seizure disorder under investigation. 

I reviewed Michael Harris in clinic today with his partner in attendance. He remains on a ketogenic/modified diet programme initiated and supervised at another centre; he brought a summary of his current macronutrient targets and typical meal plan, which I have scanned to our records. He reports consistent adherence, with occasional adjustments advised by the dietetic team following periodic ketone monitoring. 

He has recorded 2 seizures to date in March, 7 in February and six in January, including nocturnal and daytime periods. He describes brief behavioural arrest with eyelid fluttering on two occasions in February, and several longer episodes with loss of awareness in January, one of which occurred after a missed meal. No recent use of rescue medication. There is no clear precipitant apart from occasional sleep restriction. No new focal neurological symptoms between events. 

Current medicines (patient-reported): lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily; levetiracetam 1 g twice daily. No recent dose changes. No adverse effects volunteered beyond mild irritability on levetiracetam; he declines a change at present. 

Examination today was unremarkable. Weight stable compared to last visit; hydration satisfactory. Routine bloods from last month (arranged by the diet team) reportedly normal, including bicarbonate and lipid profile; we have requested copies. 

Plan: 
- Continue current antiepileptic regimen without change for now. 
- Maintain the externally supervised ketogenic/modified diet; we will liaise with the supervising team to share seizure logs and request periodic metabolic panels (including lipids, LFTs, FBC, U&Es). 
- He will continue daily seizure recording with date, time, context (sleep, meals, stress), and any magnet/rescue use; he will bring logs to next review. 
- Provide written information on sleep hygiene and illness-management strategies as potential modifiers of event frequency. 
- Safety counselling reviewed today (driving not applicable, swimming with supervision only, avoidance of heights and open flames during periods of increased events). 
- Arrange follow-up in three months, or sooner if frequency increases or events change in character. 

Yours sincerely
